summary: Initial cost/unit economics intake with LedgerBridge. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for an LLM-powered transaction summarization feature. Main topics: per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, latency SLOs vs budget constraints, reserved capacity estimate for sustained QPS, and pilot next steps.
transcript:
Date: 2026-03-08 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~49 minutes

Header: Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nanda (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood Solutions), Aisha Patel (LedgerBridge CTO), Tom Reynolds (Lead ML Eng), Mei Chen (Platform)

[00:00] Jordan Kim: Heyyyy, thanks everyone for taking the time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, I'm the account lead here. Quick introductions?
[00:08] Aisha Patel: Hi, Aisha here, CTO at LedgerBridge. We're trying to get a better sense of cost levers for inference — like per-token, batching, caching — and where dedicated or private makes sense versus hosted.
[00:18] Tom Reynolds: Tom — I lead ML infra. We have a fairly predictable nightly batch and daytime interactive traffic, roughly 20 rps peak today, hoping to scale to 150 rps in 6 months.
[00:27] Mei Chen: Mei, platform, will own networking and security for any private deployment.
[00:32] Priya Nanda: Priya from Redwood SE. We'll dig into workload shapes and give a realistic TCO.
[00:36] Marcus Li: Marcus, solutions, happy to walk through numbers and what we can pilot.

[01:02] Jordan Kim: Cool. High level context — LedgerBridge wants to add an intelligent transaction summarizer that expands and classifies user statements, so typical prompt lengths are 500-1,200 tokens and responses average 300-700 tokens. Is that right Tom?
[01:12] Tom Reynolds: Yeah that's the ballpark. Also a lot of short retriever context inserts — so some requests are 2k context+short response.

[01:40] Priya Nanda: Ok, good. Two things that drive unit cost: per-token spend (model compute) and how much of that you can avoid with caching/prefix reuse. For hosted, rough example pricing — and caveat this is illustrative — say model X at hosted might be $0.002 per 1K input tokens and $0.004 per 1K output tokens. But really depends on exact model and size.
[01:58] Aisha Patel: Sorry can you run that back? $0.002 per what?
[02:02] Priya Nanda: Per 1,000 input tokens; it's 0.002 USD per 1K input tokens and 0.004 USD per 1K generated tokens in this example. So a 1,000-in/500-out call would be ~0.003 total. We will share the up-to-date hosted price sheet.
[02:18] Tom Reynolds: That's helpful. How does batching change that math? We get billed per compute, right?

[02:25] Marcus Li: Right — batching mainly reduces GPU utilization inefficiencies; think of it as amortizing kernel overhead across multiple sequences. If your inferred workload has spikes that can be batched without breaking latency SLOs, effective $/token can drop 15-50% depending on batch sizes and sequence length.
[02:42] Mei Chen: But batching increases tail latency, yes? For user-facing features we have 200ms p95 target.
[02:48] Priya Nanda: Exactly, there's a tradeoff. Continuous batching on the runtime tries to keep latency under SLOs by forming small, fast batches. For a 200ms p95, you'll likely keep small batch sizes — marginal gains but still useful — maybe 10-20% cost improvement. For background jobs you can accept larger batching and get much bigger savings.

[03:18] Aisha Patel: We also have compliance concerns — can we run in our VPC? Data residency?
[03:23] Jordan Kim: Yep. Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) gives you control over networking and KMS, plus audit logs. There's an onboarding/licensing fee for private plus support contract. Hedging between private and dedicated: dedicated is still managed by us but gives reserved capacity and data separation; private gives you the control plane in your VPC.

[03:45] Tom Reynolds: Cost-wise, ballpark how much for dedicated reserved vs hosted for our target of say 150 rps sustained?
[03:53] Priya Nanda: A rough way to think about it: hosted is pure usage. If you look at a sustained high QPS, dedicated's breakeven comes when your monthly compute spend on hosted exceeds the committed capacity cost. For example, a small dedicated pool (2 x A100-class nodes equivalent) might start around $15k–$25k/month reserved depending on SLA, scaling, and contract. If your hosted monthly spend approaches or exceeds that, dedicated becomes attractive.
[04:17] Marcus Li: Also note burst capacity and autoscaling: dedicated can have configurable burst to hosted, so you don't need to size for the absolute peak if that peak is rare.

[04:34] Mei Chen: We currently forecast monthly token volume ~200M tokens. Do you have a quick calc of what that would look like hosted vs dedicated?
[04:41] Priya Nanda: Sure, hand-wave calc: if average cost is $0.003 per 1K tokens combined (input+output weighted), then 200M tokens is 200,000 * 0.003 = $600/month ??? Wait, that's off — let me recalc in-line — 200M tokens is 200,000 K tokens. Multiply 200,000 * $0.003 = $600. That can't be right for our earlier per-1K numbers, hold on.
[05:04] Tom Reynolds: Yeah I thought that seemed low.
[05:07] Priya Nanda: Sorry math slip — let's do it clean. If it's $0.003 per 1K tokens, then per token is 0.000003. Multiply by 200,000,000 tokens = $600. Hmm that's correct arithmetically, but our earlier per-1K numbers were higher for model X: 0.002 + 0.004 combined example could be 0.006 per 1K tokens. Use model-specific. If combined is 0.006 per 1K, then 200,000 * 0.006 = $1,200. Still small — looks like our example rates are small because they're per-1K.
[05:34] Aisha Patel: So hosted for our 200M tokens is like ~$1k–2k per month in your example? That seems unexpectedly low versus our infra expectations.
[05:43] Marcus Li: Two reasons numbers look small: 1) per-1K pricing scales, and 200M tokens is not enormous relative to model costs; 2) for latency-sensitive interactive usage you should include overheads — networking, request overheads, and the fact that larger models have much higher per-token costs. Also embedding and retrieval costs are additional.
[06:04] Tom Reynolds: We plan to use a 20B-ish decoder model, does Redwood host models in that class and what's the delta?
[06:10] Priya Nanda: Yes, we host multiple open models and quantized variants. Larger models typically 2-5x per-token cost of base model. So pick the model and we can give a more accurate spot rate. Also quantized 4-bit variants reduce VM cost significantly and lower per-token compute cost by ~30-50% in many cases depending on kernel support.

[06:40] Aisha Patel: For a production rollout we need hard numbers to compare to running our own cluster — we have on-prem hardware budget estimates and ops cost.
[06:49] Jordan Kim: Understood. Typically customers request a Dedicated Pilot — we provision a small reserved pool, run your prompt set under our observability and give a per-token and per-inference breakdown, plus a recommended quantization and batching config. That outputs a pilot TCO document.

[07:09] Mei Chen: How long does a pilot take and what's the cost?
[07:12] Marcus Li: Usually 1-2 weeks to stand up and run a representative benchmark. Redwood sometimes credits part of the pilot cost if it converts to committed capacity. We can do a scoped quick probe in a couple of days too.

[07:28] Tom Reynolds: In terms of caching — we've got a lot of repetition: same merchant descriptions, same categories — would prefix or KV caching help?

[07:34] Priya Nanda: Yes, prefix and KV cache can be huge. If your conversation/context or the prompt has large shared prefixes, caching avoids re-computing earlier layers and KV cache hit rates can reduce forward compute by 30-70% for repetitive content. You'd still pay for the tokens we store in cache replication but you avoid full compute. We can estimate hit-rate from a sample prompt set.

[07:58] Aisha Patel: Are there storage costs for KV cache or any extra licensing?
[08:02] Priya Nanda: There's minimal incremental storage cost; it's part of the runtime. For private/on-prem you manage the storage. For hosted/dedicated we include it, but large persistent caches tied to long documents may have additional charges if they exceed standard quotas. We'll flag that in the TCO.

[08:20] Tom Reynolds: Latency — our frontend needs p95 under 300ms for most user flows. Are the batching gains incompatible with that?
[08:28] Priya Nanda: If p95 300ms is a hard SLO, batching will be conservative. Continuous batching can still give micro-batching improvements (10-20%) while keeping p95. The bigger savings are for background or eventual consistency paths. Also you can serve small models for the hottest traffic and route complex requests to larger models — that's a routing policy we support.

[08:52] Mei Chen: Network egress and transfer for hosted — we have customers in EU, need data residency. Will data leave region?
[08:59] Jordan Kim: We have region controls. For hosted accounts you can pin region; for private we can guarantee in-VPC control. We'll share data residency doc and SOC2 details as requested.

[09:14] Aisha Patel: Can we estimate a per-conversation cost example? E.g., a typical user session has 3 calls: two short 100-token queries and one long 800-token gen.
[09:23] Marcus Li: Sure. Example numbers: assume combined effective rate $0.006 per 1K tokens (again model dependent). Two short 100-token queries (300 tokens total) + 800 = 1,100 tokens per session. 1.1 * ($0.006 per 1K) => 1,100 tokens is 1.1 K tokens, cost = 1.1 * 0.006 = $0.0066 per session. If caching covers say 40% of tokens you can drop to ~ $0.004/session.
[09:49] Tom Reynolds: So even at scale that seems manageable — 1M monthly sessions would be $6k? That math seems favorable compared to infra.

[10:00] Priya Nanda: Right, but keep in mind model selection affects cost steps: a 70B model may be 3-6x more expensive. Also throughput concerns — serving 150 rps at low latency may require more reserved capacity.

[10:22] Aisha Patel: On dedicated pricing — you mentioned 15k–25k per month for small pool. What is included — is that purely compute or support and SLOs too?
[10:31] Priya Nanda: Dedicated typically includes compute reservation, monitoring, basic support, and a baseline SLA. Higher SLA and longer retention in observability are add-ons. Private deployments add licensing and dedicated support. We'll outline these in the sheet.

[10:48] Mei Chen: If we commit to a year, are there discounts?
[10:51] Jordan Kim: Yes, annual commitments get discounts; multi-year deeper. Also commit to capacity for burst credits and lower unit pricing. We'll put example tiered pricing in the doc.

[11:05] Tom Reynolds: Any gotchas on quantization impacting quality?
[11:09] Priya Nanda: Some prompts, especially generation with long coherent paragraphs, can show slight degradation at aggressive quantizations. We recommend A/B evaluation on your prompt set. We usually run mixed-precision: quantize where safe, keep FP for critical layers if needed.

[11:28] Aisha Patel: Security audit — Mei will want SOC2 and SSO integration details.
[11:33] Mei Chen: Yep, SAML/SSO, RBAC, KMS integration are must-haves. Also encrypted logs and audit trails.

[11:41] Jordan Kim: We'll send the security pack and an overview of SSO/KMS flows. We can also provide an architecture sketch for private deployment.

[11:55] Tom Reynolds: For the pilot, we want to validate both latency and cost. Can Redwood run benchmark with our prompt set and simulate production QPS?
[11:59] Marcus Li: Yes — pilot sequence: 1) get prompt set + traffic profile 2) spin up a small dedicated pool or scoped hosted instances 3) run workload and collect per-call cost, latency histogram, and cache hit metrics 4) produce a TCO and rollout recommendation.

[12:20] Aisha Patel: Who owns the test infra for the pilot? We prefer Redwood to run it but with our data in a secure way.
[12:26] Priya Nanda: We can run it in a dedicated sandbox account with restricted access; or if you prefer private, we can provide a deployable package.

[12:40] Mei Chen: One more Q on billing buckets — do you break out token compute from networking and caching charges?
[12:45] Jordan Kim: Yes, the Console shows token-level cost, model cost, and infrastructure. We can export per-route breakdowns.

[12:55] Tom Reynolds: Any recommendation on routing policy — like cold path to 70B, hot path to 7B?
[12:59] Priya Nanda: Common pattern: hot small models for top 80% low-latency traffic, fallback to larger for complex cases; probabilistic sampling for quality monitoring. This keeps unit cost down. We'll show sample routing configs.

[13:18] Aisha Patel: OK. On the pricing doc please show: 1) hosted per-token for 3 model tiers 2) dedicated reserved cost examples for 2 pool sizes 3) expected per-session cost examples with/without caching and quantization 4) pilot scoping and time/cost to run.
[13:34] Jordan Kim: Noted. We'll send that pack.

[13:45] Mei Chen: One operational question — how do you handle KV cache invalidation across updates to our taxonomy?
[13:50] Priya Nanda: Cache invalidation can be policy-driven — time-to-live, explicit invalidation calls, or namespace versioning. We can integrate hooks into your deployment pipeline.

[14:02] Tom Reynolds: For the pilot, can we get cost estimates per 10k sessions?
[14:06] Marcus Li: Yes, we'll include per-10k and per-100k session examples with different hit rates and model choices.

[14:17] Aisha Patel: Great. Any blockers on our side to get started?
[14:21] Jordan Kim: We need the prompt sample, traffic profile, and a signed NDA if you'd like the private doc. Otherwise we'll start with hosted/dedicated numbers.

[14:29] Tom Reynolds: I'll share the prompt set and QPS spreadsheet by Wednesday.
[14:33] Mei Chen: I'll loop in security and legal for the NDA.

[14:40] Jordan Kim: Thanks — recap of next steps: we'll send pricing/TCO spreadsheet, security pack, and propose pilot dates (tentative 2026-03-18). Priya will scope a quick perf probe.

[14:53] Aisha Patel: Thanks everyone.
[14:56] Jordan Kim: Appreciate it. End of call.

Notes: transcript has some minor transcription miss-words (e.g., "breakeven" transcribed as "break even" in places) and occasional run-ons as typical of Fireflies exports. References shared: pricing sheet (link omitted), security pack (link omitted), pilot TCO template (link omitted).
